summary: Why an implementation plan is essential and how to write one — tasks, timeline, resources, data conversion, training, testing and risks.

theory.title: Why an implementation plan is important

blocks.content: A document that sets out **how, when and by whom** the new system will be installed and put into use: the tasks, their order and timing, resources, training, data transfer, testing and risk management.

items: Ensures **no task is forgotten** (hardware, software, data, training, documentation).
Puts tasks in the **right order** and shows **dependencies** (data cannot be transferred before the database is installed).
Sets **deadlines** and assigns **responsibilities**, so progress can be monitored.
Estimates **cost and resources**, keeping the project within budget.
Minimises **disruption** to the organisation's normal work.
Identifies **risks** and fallback actions in advance.

blocks.title: Contents of the plan
rows: Direct / parallel / pilot / phased, with justification
Computers, network, printers, servers — who installs, when
Moving existing data into the new system; checking it (verification)
Acceptance testing with real users and data
Who is trained, how (courses, manuals, videos), when
User guide, technical documentation handed over
Tasks with start/end dates — often a **Gantt chart**
What could go wrong and the backup plan

blocks.title: Example plan — new library system at a school (pilot method)
rows: Install and configure the library software
Enter book records and scan barcodes
Pilot: Grade 11 students borrow with the new system
Roll out to the whole school

blocks.content: A good plan answer lists the **steps in a logical order**, gives each a **time and a person**, and states the **changeover method** with a reason.
